content: Palliative care services can be effectively integrated into primary healthcare and home-care services using a community-based approach. It is estimated that less than 20% of advanced cancer patients will require highly specialized palliative care services. These specialized services can be delivered through palliative care units located in district hospitals or tertiary-level facilities. Inpatient and outpatient palliative care clinics at secondary and tertiary levels primarily function as training and referral centers for managing complex cases and supervising other levels of care. Cancer palliative care services should be closely integrated with cancer prevention, early detection, and treatment services, as well as with other related programs and initiatives. A team-based approach is essential, with strong leadership and comprehensive program management ensuring that local managers and healthcare providers work collaboratively in multidisciplinary teams across the healthcare system. These teams should also coordinate closely with community leaders and organizations involved in the program to achieve shared goals. The composition of a palliative care team varies depending on the program's objectives and the availability of healthcare professionals. Generally, palliative care requires a robust network of trained healthcare practitioners, community leaders, traditional healers, and family caregivers, each with specific roles and responsibilities across different levels of care and within the community. Healthcare providers involved in palliative care may include physicians, nurses, social workers, psychologists, spiritual counselors, volunteers, pharmacists, and traditional healers. Each plays a critical role in delivering comprehensive care. Physicians are central to interdisciplinary palliative care teams. They must be skilled in general medicine, pain and symptom management, and the principles of disease management. Physicians are often responsible for assessing, supervising, and managing complex treatment dilemmas. They also lead interdisciplinary teams and play a vital educational role by discussing medical management decisions and integrating research findings into practice. In resource-limited settings, where physician availability is low, incorporating palliative care into the services provided by all doctors treating cancer patients (e.g., gynecologists, surgeons, radiotherapists, pediatricians) and including it in undergraduate medical curricula can ensure broader, though less specialized, coverage. Nurses are typically the team members with the most prolonged contact with patients. This extended interaction allows nurses to deeply understand the patient and their caregivers, assess their needs, and help them cope with the effects of advancing disease. Nurses are experts in providing physical and emotional care, managing symptoms, educating patients and families, and organizing the patient’s environment to minimize loss of control. In some settings, where physicians are scarce, nurses may lead multidisciplinary teams and oversee all aspects of palliative care. In such cases, nurses require specialized training tailored to the cultural and economic context in which they work. Nurses also play a role in public and volunteer education about palliative care. Social workers and psychologists assist patients and families in addressing the personal and social challenges of illness and disability. They provide support during disease progression and the bereavement process. Social workers assess the psychosocial needs of patients and families, anticipate potential family dysfunction or financial difficulties, and offer interventions such as referrals to community services, emotional support, individual counseling, and bereavement counseling. Spiritual counselors provide support by addressing existential questions about the meaning of life, which often arise for patients and their families. They act as skilled, non-judgmental listeners, helping patients reflect on their past and prepare for the future. For those with religious traditions, spiritual counselors may organize meaningful rituals and sacraments. Training in end-of-life care is essential for spiritual counselors. Volunteers play diverse roles within palliative care teams, depending on the setting. In lowand middle-resource settings, volunteers may provide most of the care for patients. They assist healthcare professionals in delivering optimal quality of life for patients and families, often serving as a link between healthcare institutions and the community. With appropriate training and support, volunteers can provide direct patient care, assist with administrative tasks, work as counselors, raise awareness, provide health education, generate funds, and even deliver some types of medical care. Pharmacists are crucial in palliative care due to the significant role of drug therapies in symptom management. Pharmacists ensure access to essential medications for patients and families and support the healthcare team by providing information on drug dosages, interactions, formulations, administration routes, and alternative approaches. In lowand middle-income countries, pharmacists with basic skills and training are vital for palliative care delivery. They can prepare analgesic medications, such as morphine, from inexpensive raw materials and manage distribution systems for home-care patients. Traditional healers are widely recognized for their role in complementary and alternative therapies, with about two-thirds of cancer patients worldwide utilizing such treatments. While traditional healers are not typically part of palliative care teams, open dialogue between healthcare providers and traditional healers can help coordinate efforts to meet patients' and families' needs in a culturally sensitive and respectful manner. Palliative care teams should be established across all levels of healthcare. At the tertiary level, all physicians and nurses treating cancer patients should receive basic training in managing pain, symptoms, and psychosocial support. Complex cases should be referred to specialized teams comprising a palliative care physician, nurse, part-time social worker or psychologist, and pharmacist. These teams also serve as national reference and training groups. At the secondary level, physicians and nurses treating cancer patients should receive basic training in pain and symptom management and psychosocial support. Complex cases are referred to specialized teams at the district level, which include a palliative care physician and/or nurse, a part-time social worker, and a pharmacist. These teams act as district reference and training groups. At the primary level, nurses treating cancer patients should receive basic training in pain and symptom management and psychosocial support. Complex cases are referred to specialized teams at secondary or tertiary levels. Primary-level specialist nurses are trained to train and supervise community leaders, family caregivers, and traditional healers. Palliative care services can be delivered through inpatient care, outpatient care, and home-based care. Inpatient care in low-income countries often relies on specialized palliative care teams rather than standalone units, which are cost-intensive. These teams, composed of a palliative care physician, clinical nurse, and part-time social worker, provide consultations and training to a large number of healthcare professionals. Outpatient care units, such as day-care centers, offer low-cost care for patients who are not too ill to attend. These units provide periodic procedures, train family caregivers, and offer respite for relatives by addressing patients' physical, psychological, and spiritual needs. Home-based care is more resource-intensive in high-income countries but is generally more acceptable and affordable in lowand middle-income countries, where patients often prefer to die at home. For example, Uganda’s Ministry of Health, with support from local NGOs, has included pain relief and palliative care in a home-care package based on patient and caregiver needs assessments. Services include essential medications for pain and symptom relief, food provision, and family support.
